extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, social scientists, and policymakers studying public opinion, propaganda, and social psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Principled guidance for recognizing and avoiding cognitive, sampling, temporal, spatial, and rhetorical errors when forming or presenting public opinion and social/political analysis. Applies to researchers, journalists, and policymakers who must generalize from evidence and engage audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes distort perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes make people interpret new facts through preconceptions so that conflicting facts are censored or 'stretched out of shape.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: wartime views (American vs French) where preconceptions made distant theatres invisible or produced phantom armies; always test whether observed facts fit an existing stereotype or genuinely challenge it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real conception of space requires practical transportation factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical map distance is not the same as the practical distance to be traversed; transportation availability, schedules, speeds, costs, and local conditions determine real accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept 'miles as the crow flies' as meaningful for travel or policy decisions; specify modes of transport, detours, road/sea/rail conditions (e.g., motor car nine miles with six miles of ruts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary drawing must reflect practical geography
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines drawn by abstract formulas (e.g., self-determination) can bisect living, economic, and social spaces, producing absurd results unless practical geography is considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When delineating territory or policy jurisdictions, check how lines affect factories, villages, markets, pastures, railheads, and daily life rather than only colored ethnic or political maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match time-conception to the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Different decisions require different time-scales (hours, weeks, decades, geological time); using the wrong time-perspective leads to error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the matter calls for short-term emergency calculation or long-run planning (examples: wartime action vs civilization-building; forest policy vs coal reserves) and justify the chosen horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of treating the long run as permanent
rubrics_metrics.description: People often assume long durations (e.g., 'ninety-nine years' or constitutional permanence) mean 'forever,' ignoring future change and the limits of imposing present norms on distant generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit prescriptive permanence (legal or institutional) and allow for amendment; treat long-term commitments as contingent and specify mechanisms for future adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use representative/random sampling, not convenience samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations about classes require properly selected samples; convenience or contact-based samples produce worthless, unrepresentative results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow neutral/random selection methods (as Sheffield social workers did on Bowley's advice) rather than recruiting via philanthropic contacts, missions, clubs, or other biased access points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure adequate sample size for desired precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical calculations determine minimum sample sizes to limit deviation (e.g., Bowley recommended 408 men and 408 women to keep deviation within 1 in 22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify sampling error and state confidence/precision goals; do not claim population-level conclusions from tiny or unspecified samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selection bias that confirms prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Casual impressions often pick samples that support pre-existing beliefs (the most troublesome or docile worker, the social circle), falsely projecting them onto whole classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively check for and correct selection bias, consider counterexamples, and avoid treating convenient anecdotes as representative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifications are partial and time-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels (e.g., 'working class') cover only part of the truth at certain times; people may move in and out of categories and subgroups may not fit the stereotype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about classification criteria, recognize heterogeneity within categories, and avoid treating an organized nucleus as identical to the whole statistical class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer causation from sequence or coincidence (post hoc ergo propter hoc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallelism or temporal sequence is often mistaken for causal connection, especially by untrained minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek independent causal evidence and rigorous analysis rather than assuming that co-occurrence implies cause and effect (examples: blaming alehouses for smallpox; linking relativity and Bolshevism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional association biases causal reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong feelings attach unrelated phenomena into causal systems; things that evoke the same emotion get linked as causes or effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize emotional grouping (everything dreaded becomes mutually explanatory), and separate affective associations from empirical causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absolutist language and thinking; use qualifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions about public affairs often need moderation; absolute words (forever, always, must, shall) mask necessary caveats and nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer qualifying adverbs (perhaps, partly, temporarily, toward) and beware of converting desirable goals into assumed present truths (the 'faith ladder').

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about projecting goals backward onto present evidence (faith ladder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire that something ought to be true can lead to selecting and weighting present evidence as if the desired end already existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid substituting the goal for the starting point; do not read future potential as present reality; follow James's ladder as a warning against presuming outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropomorphism and exaggerated personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: We habitually personify collective forces (Social Movements, Economic Forces) and dramatize relations, which can simplify but also misrepresent complex systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using allegory or personification, be conscious of the metaphor's limits, and ensure analysis distinguishes individual agency from systemic descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage audiences by clear identification and strong themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular representation requires marked heroes and clear choices; audiences need an active role (exercised by potent themes like sexual passion and fighting) to be engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For journalism or popular media, make the hero/villain clear, provide opportunities for audience participation or emotional engagement, and use compelling themes responsibly to avoid stereotype exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow proper time-sequence for capacity-building and institutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals that expect immediate large-scale change (e.g., instant industrial democratization) ignore the varied time requirements for learning and training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design programs so assumption of responsibility parallels training and preparation; resist sudden imposition of roles that realistically take years to develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for resource time-scales in policy (intergenerational equity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural resources differ in formation time (trees vs coal); sound policy computes reserves, use rates, alternatives, and selects a justified intergenerational horizon for stewardship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute available reserves, projected usage, efficiency measures, and decide how many future generations constitute 'posterity' when setting standards for conservation or development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize vividness and discrimination affect perceived duration and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Vividness (number of discriminations perceived) alters how events feel in duration and in memory; active events feel longer in recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public perceptions of historical or recent events, account for how vivid experiences distort perceived time and importance; avoid treating vivid anecdotes as proportional evidence.
